llm.summary: The skill appears to implement a P2P Portal and its local bridge/installer as described, but it asks for and uses sensitive credentials (SSH private keys, OpenClaw hooks token), references reading other OpenClaw config files, auto-processes tokens from messages, and includes insecure defaults — these behaviors are coherent with the feature set but raise notable security and scope concerns.

dimensions.detail: Name/description (Agent P2P Portal + Bridge) match the code and instructions: python3, ssh, API Key, Hub URL, and OpenClaw hooks token are reasonably required for deploying a Portal on a VPS and running a local bridge. Requiring SSH and deployment scripts is expected for the described deploy-to-VPS workflow.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: Runtime instructions and code go beyond simple message sending: they ask the agent/user to read ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json for hooks.token, run install/deploy scripts that perform SSH operations, and start persistent bridge processes. The client code automatically parses messages for verification codes and tokens and will call back to the OpenClaw gateway (hooks/wake) with extracted content — this could surface secrets unexpectedly. SKILL.md also instructs copying the skill into the workspace and running startup scripts that will persist long-running processes.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no registry 'install' spec; code and scripts are bundled. The provided install.py and scripts/deploy_portal.py will execute local actions and SSH into a VPS via the user's key. The install uses pip to install paramiko at runtime, and deploy scripts reference a GitHub repo; these are typical but mean arbitrary remote deployment commands will run if you execute them. No remote binary download URL shorteners or IP-only downloads were found in the provided excerpts.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill requests/uses sensitive variables: AGENTP2P_API_KEY and AGENTP2P_HUB_URL (expected), but also OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_URL and OPENCLAW_HOOKS_TOKEN which allow the skill to wake and interact with the user's OpenClaw gateway. The docs additionally instruct reading ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json for hooks.token (a file outside the skill). The installer asks for an SSH private key path and will use it to access your VPS. These high-privilege secrets are plausible for the stated purpose but are significant and could be misused if the code is malicious or if defaults are left unchanged.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: always:false (normal). The skill runs persistent bridge/client processes and the installer configures a systemd service on the VPS (not on the local host) — that grants long-term persistence on the deployed server. Locally the skill writes state and notification files under the skill directory and ~/.openclaw. The skill does not declare unsolicited modifications to other skills, but it does rely on hooks token to wake OpenClaw sessions.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
What to consider before installing or running this skill:

1) Review code before executing: the package includes installers and remote-deploy scripts (install.py, scripts/deploy_portal.py) that SSH to servers and create services — read those files completely before running them.

2) Don't hand over your primary SSH private key: if you must deploy, create a dedicated, limited-delegation SSH key or temporary deployment key for the VPS (or perform the deploy steps manually on the server) rather than giving the skill full access to an existing private key with broad permissions.

3) Inspect and rotate sensitive defaults: the project documents default admin password and hard-coded SECRET_KEY in service unit files. If you deploy, change default admin credentials immediately and replace any hard-coded secrets.

4) Confirm how tokens are handled: the client code will parse messages for verification codes and JWT-like tokens and will call the OpenClaw gateway /hooks/wake with message content (which can expose tokens to the gateway). Only provide OPENCLAW_HOOKS_TOKEN if you trust the skill and the gateway destination; consider limiting the gateway's scope or using a token with minimal privileges.

5) Check for hidden/obfuscated content: the static scan flagged base64-blocks. Search the repository for encoded payloads or unexpected remote endpoints before running any installers or long-running processes.

6) Prefer manual deployment for higher assurance: if you control the VPS, consider running the deploy scripts step-by-step yourself (or use the included scripts but review and run the SSH commands manually) to avoid giving a script automated SSH access.

7) Least privilege and backups: limit permissions on created accounts, back up any important data, and be prepared to revoke API keys and SSH keys if something looks suspicious after testing.

If you want, I can: (a) point to specific files/lines that extract tokens or call hooks.wake, (b) scan the omitted/truncated files for encoded content, or (c) produce a short checklist of exact code snippets to audit prior to executing installers.
llm.findings: [base64-block] unexpected: The static scanner flagged a base64-block in SKILL.md. The visible SKILL.md excerpts don't contain obvious base64 payloads, so this may be a false positive or an obfuscated block elsewhere in the full package; since obfuscated payloads are uncommon for this type of skill, treat this as suspicious and inspect the full files for hidden/encoded content before running.
